diagnosis.reason: A bounded semantic inventory finds adequate vertical-overhead and roll concepts but no substantive non-aerial moderate-downward tabletop axis option. Three-quarter facial views and body rotation are not replacements. The principal weakness is a real data gap in camera-owned pitch/plane relations; baseline ranking evidence is recorded separately when available and cannot turn neighboring meanings into equivalent sources.

existing_candidates.meaning: Near-vertical downward view of a table plane.
existing_candidates.source_excerpt: The camera looks nearly vertically down onto the table plane.
existing_candidates.limitation: Directly supports overhead, not a moderate downward axis. Existing contextual definition explicitly separates vertical and oblique elevated viewpoints.

existing_candidates.meaning: Vertical optical axis over a flat selected surface.
existing_candidates.source_excerpt: The camera axis points straight down over the selected surface.
existing_candidates.limitation: Adequate overhead option; adding another overhead synonym would duplicate it.

existing_candidates.meaning: Eye-height oblique view of facial frontal and lateral planes.
existing_candidates.source_excerpt: At eye height, an oblique view shows both the frontal and lateral planes of the face.
existing_candidates.limitation: Three-quarter names a facial azimuth relation here, not downward tabletop pitch; also fixes eye height.
Direction is relevant but bound to aerial capture wording; weak as a tabletop still-life axis description and has no visible plane relation detail.

existing_candidates.meaning: Camera roll measured through stable scene reference lines.
existing_candidates.source_excerpt: the camera roll rotates a stable scene reference relative to the image axes
existing_candidates.limitation: Useful roll boundary but existing record requires human context and main portrait; does not supply downward pitch.

existing_candidates.meaning: Subject torso and shoulders rotate relative to camera.
existing_candidates.source_excerpt: the torso and shoulder plane turn obliquely to the camera
existing_candidates.limitation: Pose effect, not camera-axis effect. A stationary camera can see this through subject rotation.

existing_candidates.meaning: Visible eye axes point toward lens independently of face orientation.
existing_candidates.source_excerpt: The visible pupils point toward the camera while head direction is stated separately.
existing_candidates.limitation: Expression/gaze effect, not capture-camera pitch or yaw.

sources.title: Canon — Cooking with the Camera: Tips for Amazing Food Photography
sources.supports: Distinguishes straight-on, three-quarter and overhead food angles; relates visible tops versus side/layers to subject form. This supports the angle boundary, not an exact universal degree.

sources.title: University at Buffalo CSE668 — 3-D Imaging Models
sources.supports: Models optical-axis orientation and camera location as separate extrinsic quantities; rotation R and translation t have distinct roles. Supports direction versus height/distance and object/world versus camera coordinates.

sources.title: Stanford CS248 — Camera position and rotation
sources.supports: Separates position from pitch, yaw and roll; roll is rotation about the viewing direction. Axis names depend on coordinate convention.

sources.title: Adobe — What is a Dutch angle shot and how is it used?
sources.supports: A canted frame makes normally horizontal or vertical scene lines diagonal. Supports roll versus pitch and subject lean; its emotional associations are optional conventions, not required effects.

confusion_boundaries.rule: Pitch is an angular relation; an elevated position alone does not specify where the optical axis points. Raising or lowering the camera and changing distance are separate translation choices.

confusion_boundaries.boundary: Three-quarter table angle versus three-quarter face/body
confusion_boundaries.rule: Table use describes downward inclination; facial/body use often describes azimuth or subject rotation. Name the reference surface and visible top/side relation.
A static final projection supplies a relative orientation, not a history of which participant moved. Do not add subject rotation or camera motion to satisfy the camera role.

Downward aim changes sightline inclination; roll rotates frame axes about the viewing direction. A diagonal table edge alone cannot establish roll because perspective and object orientation also create diagonals.
An actor looking downward or toward the lens says where the eyes point. Neither determines capture-camera direction.
A perpendicular plan and a steep inclined axis are distinct. Side visibility depends jointly on camera position and object geometry; it is supporting evidence, not a unique angle measurement.

Three-quarter is a photographic convention with context-dependent use; the sources do not justify an exact universal 45-degree requirement. No exact angle, height, focal length or distance is prescribed.

recommendations: Integrate the four distinct authored axis records only after source review; retain existing adequate strict-overhead options.
Keep original query bytes and common-pool H-F2 weights/ranking unchanged for before/after tests.
Review all returned top8 full sources for camera ownership; do not count body rotation, eye gaze, aerial capture or overhead as direct moderate-downward tabletop success.

Conditions use existing object and scene tags as conservative discovery guards. A real existing horizontal surface, and front/side faces for the level product case, must be independently established by the requester core and native guard/owner review before adoption. The records do not create those owners, surfaces, object geometry or camera position.
Treat every addition as discovery-only. Native semantic qualification and optional adoption remain unperformed; effects are camera direction only.

baseline_review.interpretation: The unchanged-query baseline exposes surrounding scene context, overhead, body rotation, eye gaze and height. These are concrete ownership/axis confusions. Because the intended substantive non-aerial tabletop relation is missing from inspected source, this remains data_gap; poor results alone do not establish a separate exposure-only failure.
